claims.text: The target material is bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
A machine-learning model will use ab initio oxygen-defect and other defect-scattering parameters as input features.
Conductivity measurements exist for the oxygen-containing alloy in the 0–200 K and 300–1200 K regimes.
Oxygen-induced defect sites modify electron-scattering events in the lattice.
Ab initio simulations can capture scattering rates and energy perturbations introduced by oxygen defects in HfNbTaTiZr.
An ML correction model can learn from multi-regime experimental data to map temperature to electrical conductivity.
Including defect-scattering features will account for defect-induced carrier-mobility changes that ideal-crystal predictions omit.
The integrated model will predict conductivity more accurately than traditional analytical models that assume perfect crystals.
The model should predict conductivity at 350 K to within ±5% of experiment.
The model should capture distinct changes in conduction mechanisms between the cryogenic and high-temperature regimes.
Existing perfect-crystal analytical predictions deviate from experiment by more than ±5% in both specified temperature regimes.
The model is applicable only to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K without further validation.
Extension to other impurity levels, alloy compositions, or the 200–300 K interval requires additional validation.
Prediction improvement and the 350 K error depend on the quality of the ab initio inputs and experimental training data.
Unaccounted defects or impurities may affect prediction accuracy.
An error exceeding ±5% at 350 K would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to reproduce the observed temperature-dependent behavior across both regimes would falsify the hypothesis.
